summary: This document specifies how a Port Control Protocol (PCP) client should contact its PCP servers when one or several server addresses are configured. It updates RFC 6887.

eli5.summary: If a program has several helpers it can ask to open a door in a firewall, this says in what order to try them.

questions: how does a pcp client choose a server
how many times does a pcp client retransmit
what is the pcp maximum retransmission count
subtitle: How a PCP client picks, retries and sticks to the right server address when it has been given several.

tldr.problem: A Port Control Protocol client may be configured with several server addresses, or with several servers, and RFC 6887 does not say in enough detail which to contact or what to do when one does not answer.
tldr.mechanism: The client sorts a server's addresses using the RFC 6724 rules, tries each with up to 4 retransmissions, moves to the next on silence or a hard ICMP error, and keeps using the first address that answers. With several servers it runs this procedure for each one.
tldr.outcome: PCP clients behave predictably when servers have several addresses or when a host is multihomed. The RFC updates RFC 6887.

today: RFC 7488 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2015. It updates RFC 6887, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Server Selection Is Needed
sections.content:
A host can have several network interfaces (the RFC mentions 3G and IEEE 802.11), each configured with different PCP servers. Each server learned must be associated with the interface on which it was learned. A single PCP server may also have several IP addresses, and multihoming is one situation where a client ends up with several server addresses.

When a client discovers several addresses, it has to decide what to do: install entries on all of them or a subset, remove some entries, and so on. The RFC makes three assumptions. Servers on the same interface need not have the same capabilities. Requests to different servers are independent, so the result of one does not influence another. The configuration mechanism must distinguish addresses that belong to the same server.

The document does not care how the addresses were configured (DHCP is given as an example) and makes no assumption about whether they are unicast or anycast.
sections.eli5: A kid might have two helpers at school, and each helper might have two phone numbers. Before asking for help, the kid needs a plan for whom to call first.

sections.title: One Server, Several Addresses
sections.content:
When one PCP server has several addresses, the client follows these steps:

  • Build a set of candidate source addresses, based on application input and PCP constraints. For a PEER, or a MAP with FILTER, for an existing TCP connection, the only candidate is that connection's source address. For a MAP for a service that accepts incoming connections, it may be all the node's addresses or the subset the service listens on.
  • Sort the server's addresses using the destination address selection rules of RFC 6724, with those candidate sources as input.
  • Set the Maximum Retransmission Count (MRC) to 4.
  • Send PCP messages following the retransmission procedure of RFC 6887. If no response arrives after MRC attempts, move on to the next address in the sorted list.

A response that arrives after the client has used up its attempts on that address SHOULD be ignored. The RFC reads such a late answer as a sign of problems on the forwarding path or in how that server instance will handle later requests. A hard ICMP error means the client MUST immediately try the next address.
sections.eli5: You put the phone numbers in the best order, call the first one a few times, and if nobody picks up you try the next. If the phone company says the number does not exist, you skip to the next straight away.

sections.title: Retrying, Sticking and Nonces
sections.content:
If the client has exhausted every address for a server, the procedure SHOULD be repeated every 15 minutes until a request is answered.

Once an address has answered, all later requests to that server go to the same address until it becomes unresponsive. When that happens, the client clears its cache of sorted destination addresses and starts again from the top.

For efficiency, the client SHOULD use the same Mapping Nonce for requests to all addresses of the same server. The nonce matters because nonce validation is performed under the Simple Threat Model of RFC 6887 to defend against some off-path attacks.
sections.eli5: If none of the numbers work, you try the whole list again every 15 minutes. Once a number works, you keep calling that one until it stops answering.

sections.title: Several Servers at Once
sections.content:
A client may be configured with several servers, each reachable on its own list of addresses. These servers need not have the same capabilities. How the lists are kept separate is implementation and deployment specific. For example, DHCP can supply several lists, each naming a distinct server (RFC 7291).

The client contacts every server using the procedure above. Unlike the nonce shared across one server's addresses, the client MUST use a different Mapping Nonce for each server, as required by RFC 6887. If the client knows each server's capabilities, it MAY contact all servers simultaneously or go through them with a delay.

The result can be several mappings held by different servers. Whether to keep all of them or delete some depends on the purpose of the request. If the servers configure firewall (not NAT) functionality, the client would by default need to use all of them, unless it knows they replicate state among themselves.
sections.eli5: If you ask several different helpers, you give each one its own secret code word. Then you decide whether you need all of their answers or just one.

sections.title: Worked Example: Two Servers, One Link
sections.content:
The RFC's example has a host on one subnet with two PCP servers, PCP-Server-A and PCP-Server-B, each co-located with an edge router (rtr1 and rtr2). Each server has an IPv4 and an IPv6 address. The client wants an IPv4 mapping, so it orders the addresses with the IPv4 one first for each server.

Suppose the path to 192.0.2.1 is broken, while the other three paths work. The client sends two requests at the same time, to 192.0.2.1 (Server A) and 198.51.100.1 (Server B). Server B answers. Server A does not, so the client retries four times, gives up on that address and tries Server A's IPv6 address, which answers. From then on the client should keep using that IPv6 address for Server A. Because the client wants IPv4 mappings, it will have to use the THIRD_PARTY option for them.
sections.eli5: One helper's first phone number is broken. You keep calling it a few times, then try the helper's second number, which works, and you stick with it from then on.

sections.title: Multihoming Scenarios
sections.content:
The appendix describes the main multihoming problem as "one PCP client, multiple PCP servers". In both examples the client learns its servers by DHCP or another provisioning mechanism and sends requests to each server in parallel.

In the IPv6 case, two or more routers with firewalls share a link with the host, and each router connects to a different provider. The host is offered several prefixes. A typical model puts a DHCP server in each router so the host can get each PCP server's addresses.

In the IPv4 case, the example is the NAT- or RFC2260-based multihoming of RFC 4116. A gateway router connects to several providers and uses NAT to translate provider-assigned addresses into one set of private addresses. Two PCP servers may then be needed, one to configure NAT toward each provider.
sections.eli5: A house with two internet providers has two doors to the outside, so the computer asks both doors' keepers for help at the same time.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: This RFC adds little of its own here. PCP security considerations are in RFC 6887. The RFC does not say how server addresses are provisioned to the client. Documents that define provisioning are responsible for explaining how to discover legitimate PCP servers.
sections.eli5: This note only says which number to call. How to be sure the number belongs to a real helper is left to whoever hands out the numbers.
